chapter: Looking back and the New York years
title: Carter as uptown saxophone, versus Kansas City jump
summary: Smith calls Carter's smooth playing uptown, compared with Willie Smith and Tab Smith.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: I'll give you a point of view of mine on Benny Carter, which you may completely disagree with, and I may be wrong. But I've listened to the man quite a lot on record, and I admire him enormously as a technician....
...and somebody who can play any chord sequence in any key.
But he doesn't, to me, sound very exciting a lot of the time. He seems to play on the beat quite a lot...
It doesn't seem to have that Kansas City jump sort of...
I mean, he doesn't excite me in the way that you do or
Well, he plays...I call it Uptown saxophone playing.
Yeah. Smooth. Uptown stuff. He don't get too far out of there on them counterpoint(?) notes.
No. Now, for instance, even taking someone like Willie Smith. I mean, I find Willie Smith a much more exciting player than Benny Carter.
He died some time ago. More than ten years ago. I don't know about Tab Smith. Is Tab Smith still alive?
No. He's dead. He's been dead about three years now.
Because he was a Texas boy, wasn't he?
No, he was from St. Louis. His home was in North Carolina, but he had been there years and years, since way back in 1932 -- he was in St. Louis. Yeah, he used to run a 12-piece

band over there. He was working around there, in St. Louis. he had the biggest band in town then, Tab Smith. I don't know whose band it was, it wasn't Tab's band, but he did arranging in there. He was one of the musicians they had in the band.
